speechtext: What reason is there for that?

subsubtopic: KINGSTON, SMITHS FALLS AND OTTAWA EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Deputations from Kingston want to be heard on the Bill.
Motion agreed to.
House in committee on Bill (No. 52) to incorporate the Nelson River Railway Company-Mr. Rutan.
This Bill has been allowed to stand over in order that it may be considered with another similar Bill containing water-powers which is not yet reported.

There are some Bills in respect to which the water is international, but they are not similar to this. The Minister of the Interior has full control of the rates for power on a river such as is referred to in this Bill.

My point is that we should have some policy by which we can protect the public interest in these waterways, and by which some revenue will be secured either to the Dominion or to the province, and some provision made by which we will not conflict with the rights of the provinces. I do not think we ought to take up any time over this to-night, as the Bill can very well stand, and when the policy of the government is declared it will go through swimmingly, I presume.

I have no objection to it standing over, because if you are going to talk it out we had better take up some other Bill. So far as this Bill is concerned the government has a policy, because Mr. GRAHAM.
for a year past the Minister of the Interior can issue licenses for a fee which goes to the revenue of the Dominion.

I have here the regulations of the Minister of the Interior and there is nothing to indicate in them what that fee is. The fixing of it is entirely in the hands of the minister, and my contention is that there should be some well defined policy, and that the fee should be fixed.
You cannot have a fixed fee.

No minister should have absolute control in these matters. For instance, if I am a personal friend of the minister I may be able to get a waterpower on more favourable terms than could another person, unless there is some well defined policy. The statement of the Minister of the Interior the other night that the regulations cover these two water-powers is not correct because they are situated in the territories, and not in the provinces, and there is no regulation covering the territories. This is a very important question. The Minister of Railways may not know' it, but the fact is that the Nelson river contains a number of great water-powers. I do not believe, that on any river in all Canada there are more water-powers than on the Nelson river. The Sea Falls alone 250,000 horse-power can be developed. There is a whole series of falls right down to the bay, and I do not think any company ought to be allowed to interfere with them. The government should keep control over them.

I know my hon. friend will agree with me when I say that it would be impossible to provide for fixed fees, because a water-power in one place may be worth only $1 per horse-power, while in another place, owing to its proximity to a populous locality, it may be worth $20 per horse-power. Some department must handle the matter, and take into consideration all the circumstances, and grant a lease by order in cojmcil after a fair rate has been fixed after full investigation.

The contention of my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) is that the power with reference to these matters should not be in the hands of a minister, but should be statutory. You can put these rights up to competition if you like, and in that way you would get over any difficulty as to fixing the fees.

I think the Minister of Railways is sufficiently broad minded to not being adverse to taking a hint from what has been done in connection with these powers in the province of British Columbia. We have a large number of very

valuable water-powers there belonging to the Crown in the right of the province, and we have a very comprehensive code dealing with them and the obtaining of rights by companies to use these water-powers. To a very large extent that province is undeveloped, and no doubt as the minister says, some water-powers are much more valuable than others. But they have, after some years of experience, deemed it wise to provide a scale of fees by order in council according to the number of cubic inches of water taken. The result is that if the power is valuable it is developed; if there is no market for it, it is not developed; but it lies there available to anybody who comes along and complies with the Act; and all are treated equally. Surely it is undesirable that it should be left to the arbitrary decision of any minister, however willing or anxious he may be to do what is right, to say what revenue should be paid by a company for the use of power. We have found the other system to work very satisfactorily, and the province derives considerable revenue from a regular tariff which anybody can ascertain without going to the minister of any department; and I should think that the same system might very profitably be adopted in connection with water-powers belonging to the Dominion.

I hope that this Bill will not be held up again to-night. The powers asked for are no more than have been granted by the Railway Committee and this House to other companies, not only in past sessions, but even in the present session. The power of expropriation has been omitted from this Bill. The Bill to which the hon. gentleman referred, the Raiuy River Company's Bill, is of an entirely different character, because it relates to the province of Ontario, where the province owns all the lands and water-powers. This Bill relates to the Northwest Territories, which belong to the Dominion, and to a portion of those territories which is undeveloped; and the people who live in that part of the country are anxious to see it developed as well as other parts of the Dominion, as they believe that it will prove to be very valuable.
Will the hon. gentle. man tell me where there any people living within a hundred miles of the proposed railway and water-power?

The people who live nearest to that country are in my own constituency. My hon. friend seems to be talking of Winnipeg and its vicinity. I ask him if there have been any petitions or communications from the city of Winnipeg against this^undertaking? We might say that it is a Winnipeg undertaking. It is for the pur-166i
pose of giving Winnipeg the cheapest and most direct connection with the Hudson Bay railway. Both the clause in the Bill giving the right of expropriation, and clause 15, with reference to a tramway, have been cut out in the Railway Committee, and it seems to me very unfair now to hold up this Bill when it asks for no more than has been granted with practically no opposition to many other companies. In the Bill that passed the Railway Committee to-day, the power given by clause 11 is practically the same as the power asked for in this Bill, and it passed the committee without any objection.
What Bill is that?

The Bill incorporating the James Bay and Eastern Railway Company. If capital is willing to go into these undeveloped territories and develop them, I do not see why we should not allow it to go there. We who live in that northern country know, from what we have heard from people who have gone into these territories and prospected, that there is untold wealth in them. It seems to me that the hon. gentlemen who are opposing this Bill are only talking against their own interests. People who live in the Northwest and who know what the development of a new country is, should be ready to receive that kindly assistance that other people are willing to give. Though the Bill is in my name, the only interest I have in it is the interest of having the country developed. I do not believe it would be possible for the Minister of the Interior, whether a Liberal or a Conservative, to grant any right or privilege to an individual or a company, that could not bear criticism. I would ask hon. gentlemen to grant this Bill fair play and give this company the same privilege as others. We are not asking for any special privileges; we are not trying to gobble up any water-powers. Neither these or any other powers which are in our rivers, whether provincial or Dominion, are of any good until they are utilized. This company asks the right to acquire water-powers and make whatever arrangement it can, either with the Department of the Interior or with the province, as the case may be.

The hon. gentleman mistakes altogether the opposition to this Bill. The Bill i3 a very simple one. It is only intended to give to a corporation the powers which an individual would have. The hon. gentleman says that they struck out the expropriation clause. They might well do that because you cannot expropriate against the Crown. I am not opposed to the Bill. I would like to see it go through, and I think it will because it is a very simple Bill giving a corporation the same powers as an individual. But

what we want is a declaration of policy from the government as to the manner in which they intend disposing of these valuable privileges, either to individuals or to corporations.

If this Bill is going to stand over, I have no intention of trying to block it, but I would point out that the matter is a very serious one. These water-powers are nearly 350 miles from Winnipeg, and there is not a white man living within one hundred and fifty or sixty miles of where this company is asking for these water-powers. The power they propose generating would be simply for the piece of railway they intend to build. They do not say where this railway is going to start. It is to start either at the mouth of the Nelson, or at the mouth of the Saskatchewan, which are 150 miles apart. The whole scheme is immature. And outside of all that is the fact that we have no regulations governing these water-powers. They are at the present outside the province, and the regulations provided by the Interior Department affect only water-powers within the different provinces. My hon. friend says that we have been giving these powers to other companies. That may be true, but that is no reason for continuing that policy. What I urge is to stay proceedings until the government investigates this matter thoroughly and brings down some policy regarding the distribution of these great water-powers. There is no question in my mind that this is 3imply a power scheme. The hon. gentleman talks about reduced rates between Winnipeg and Hudson bay, but every man who knows anything about Lake Winnipeg, knows that it is frozen up six months in the year, and in the other six months we have the water route. This is simply a scheme to control the great water-powers. If the rights of the people are protected, I have no objection to this Bill, but I do want to see their rights safeguarded. Another question is this. Within a very short time these great powers will likely come within the territory of Manitoba. The argument is used that Manitoba has no rights in her waterways; but I hope the day is not far distant when all that will be remedied. Our province should have control of our great water-powers. I believe the time is coming when Manitoba will have the control of its fisheries. That control is essential to her development and the proper protection of our fisheries. That is one of the .reasons why this government should stay its hand. I do not think we should give away rights, or any thing that may affect the future of any province. There can be no question that the province of Manitoba will have those rights in years to come, and nothing should be done here to make it impossible or difficult for the province to legislate with regard to her water-powers. I am Mr. JOHN HAGGJ RT.
not holding up the Bill, or objecting to it on personal grounds, but I realize my position, representing a constituency more directly affected than any other, as these powers are at the head of Lake Winnipeg.

I see in the Ottawa ' Free Press ' to-night that an impassable muskeg on the Hudson Bay railway route, extending many miles, has stopped the survey work. Last year I explained, in a speech I made on the twelfth of March in this House, about this muskeg, f explained that there were miles of that Hudson Bay railway route composed of frozen muskeg, covered with a kind of moss two feet, or three feet thick. This acts like sawdust in an ice house, and keeps the muskeg frozen all the year round. So long as the ground remains frozen underneath, the muskeg is passable, but as soon as it is broken up as it must be in building a railway the heat gets in, and the ground thaws out, and (the whole road-bed sinks into the muskeg. If the route of the Hudson Bay railway is to be changed, it would be well to let the Bill before us stand because, the company it proposes to incorporate is to connect with the Hudson Bay road. I think it would be as well, therefore, to let it stand over until the hon. minister gets more particulars.
A trial line should be run at once between Prince Albert city and Hudson bay to see if a better route cannot be obtained for the Hudson Bay railway. The lakes in thePascountry are so nearly on a level with the land that the water backs up, and soaks over an immense territory, and that is what causes the muskeg. I was told in Prince Albert last year that a million muskrat skins had been taken out of that country during last winter, which would indicate that there must be a considerable extent of low land there. If that be the case, I am afraid that any attempt to build a road through that section of country will be a failure, and as the road mentioned in this Bill is to connect with the Hudson Bay railway, it would be well to hold it over for reconsideration. A trial line from Prince Albert should be run at once because there are no high hills, impassable muskegs, big rivers, or other serious obstacles to be met with between northern Prince Albert; and Hudson bay.

I must urge that this matter stand over. It seems to me as if there were some concerted action to monopolize this territory. We had a Bill the other day, a canal Bill, but it was really a water-power Bill, to build a canal upon the streams reaching all the way between Lake Superior and Lake Winnipeg. This Bill is a railway Bill in name, but it is really a water-power Bill, as has been set forth by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury). I would call the atten-

tion of the House to the part of it which defines the line of railway. Under section 7 the railway is to start at Grand Rapids (at the mouth of the Saskatchewan) or at the outlet of Lake Winnipeg (that is, the Nelson river) or at any point between. One of these points is in the north east of Lake Winnipeg and the other is in the northwest. And there is at least 100 miles, perhaps 150 miles, between them. Does the railway run north, south, east or west? The Bill does not say. It runs to intersect the Hudson Bay railway, wherever it may be located by the government. That road is not located yet. So? as the hon. member for Selkirk has said, it has no starting point and it ends nowhere. That is the railway part of the Bill. It is just possible by giving that a liberal construction that the road may run all the way down the banks of the Nelson river to somewhere near York factory. And, with the powers in the original Bill-I have forgotten just how far the Bill was amended-to build tramways around the rapids-
That is cut out.

That is cut out. Well, it can run all along the Nelson Tiver for hundreds of miles. The province of Manitoba looks forward to the time when this territory will be included within its boundaries, and we would like, when this territory comes to Manitoba, that it should come unencumbered by legislation of this kind. We find that already a good deal of the puDlic domain has been alienated. We would not like to acquire this new territory and find a practical, grafting politician-well, that is too strong a word; I will take that back-sitting upon every waterfall that is among the few assets we have left. If there were any immediate necessity for the construction of this road, we should be the last [DOT]to oppose it. As the hon. member for Selkirk has said, there are not fifty white men between Lake Winnipeg and the proposed terminus of this road at York factory or any other part of that territory. If the gentleman is ready with his friends and their capital to eo ahead and develop that territory he will find not only the people of Winnipeg but the people of Manitoba behind him. But they would like to have some more definite scheme than this.

If the hon. gentleman will allow me to ask him a question? Does he understand the law at present to be such that, if this territory were added to Manitoba under the present conditions, the province of Manitoba would control the water-powers?
We have the minister-
I am asking the. hon. member for Winnipeg (A. Haggart). If he does not wish to answer, all right.

The law is by no means clear on that point. There are few water-powers in Manitoba as the province exists. It is a ' prairie province,' a level province. The only water-powers of any importance are those on the Winnipeg river in the eastern part of the province. They have been administered in this way: Parties have applied to this government for a license or a lease of the falls, or the right to develop the water-powers upon that river. But what the authority of this government is. I am not very clear.
One more question, if I may be permitted. In the case of the Win-nipeg^ river, has the province of Manitoba exercised any jurisdiction over these water-powers?
They have to this extent, that they have granted charters to people to develop these powers, and the city of Winnipeg-
That is the incorporating of a company, but have they exercised any powers or rights of ownership over the water-powers themselves?
I am not aware that they have. A water-power is a peculiar kind of property.
It is very simple.

With reference to Winnipeg river, if the Dominion owned the land all along that river no doubt the Dominion would own the lands under the river, and would have a sufficient grip upon that water-power to control it.
It would seem so.

But, if the Dominion had alienated these lands along the river- and they have alienated a lot of them, for some of these lands are what are known as swamp lands and have been conveyed to Manitoba and are Crown lands in the right of the province of Manitoba-or if they had been patented either to the province of Manitoba or to individuals who are now riparian owners, and if these held and own sufficient of the fee simple on both sides of the river, I have no doubt that, as riparian owners, they would have the right, perhaps, to develop that power in so far as that development did not interfere with navigation. But, with reference to navigation, while there are stretches in that river that are navigable for ten or twenty miles, it is not valuable as a navigable river. We do not -want to do anything to prevent development, but I -would urge upon the government to have this

Bill stand over until we know a little more -about it.
It seems to me that the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. A. Hag-gart) has shown a good deal of feeling in this matter. He speaks of grafting along _ the river-
I took that back.

The hon. gentleman makes a point of the fact that Lake Winnipeg is open only part of the year, and infers from that fact that this must be a water-power Bill entirely. But there are many things in this country not operated all the year and that yet pay dividends. Lake Superior is not open all the year. If we go back to our farmers, we find that many of them own binders, costing them up to $200, which they use for only ten days in the year. And one individual, or a number of individuals clubbing together, will buy a threshing machine at a cost of several thousand dollars, for use only about sixty days a year, and still the use of these articles are the foundation of our wealth. There is nothing in this Bill that can authorize any m in to state that it is only a power Bill. This is an undertaking to build the Tailway, and, in connection therewith, making an arrangement to build steamers to ply in connection with it, to acquire power for the undertaking and to dispose of the surplus power. This is a concession which _ is given to other companies-has been given to other companies since this Bill started through the Railway Committee. I cannot see what will be gained by putting the Bill off. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) said that this was hundreds of miles away from settlement; then he turns round and says that it is so valuable that it should be given all the protection possible, and we should wait and see what arrangement can be made with the province of Manitoba. I don't think that is the right stand to take. If we do not carry on works of development in any of the provinces until they have developed all their natural resources, we shall witness continued stagnation.

In answer to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Rutan), I would like to say that when this matter was under discussion the other evening, some question was raised about the authority of the province over these powers. The minister stated, I think, in reply to something I said myself, that even if the boundaries of the province were extended, the province would have no more rights than it has at present. We all understand that. But the point I raised was this: While 1 recognize the fact that we have at present no authority over our water-powers, I believe the time is coming when Manitoba will have control over its water-powers and Mr A. HAGGART
over its lands; and in view of that fact, 1 think the government ought to go very slow in giving control of a power where there is absolutely no necessity. There is nothing urgent, there is no present need of developing that power. If a charter was ''givbn to it, I am satisfied that there is nothing to warrant the expenditure this Bill contemplates. By the mere fact oi giving that charter we tie up that_ waterpower, which I think is a wrong principle. Now, in the interest of Manitoba, I feel that I must urge	the government to defer this Bill. I do not want to be considered as blocking the measure, but I feel that there should first be formulated some well defined policy regulating the powers on the Winnipeg river, as well as at the head of Lake Winnipeg. In answer to a question with regard to the Winnipeg river, I said that the province has some power over that river. It obtained that power largely through the fact that the swamp lands which came under its authority gave it* some rights along that river. There was a charter, I think, granted by the Dominion, but although it was granted by the Dominion, they had to seek some powers in the province of Manitoba before they could do anything with that power. Now we have 15 or 16 immense powers on that river, and if the schemes that are before parliament are allowed to go through, it would be a serious matter for that western country. On the Winnipeg river, there is no canal scheme that it is possible to carry out without injuring every water-power along that route. But I do not think myself that there is anything very serious contemplated in regard to a canal scheme. The scheme is to get control of these powers, there is no question about that; and that is one of the reasons why I have taken such strong ground against granting the powers these companies are asking for. If we grant the company in the Bill that is under discussion now, the powers that are asked for, I am satisfied that for years to come nothing could be done there in the way of development.
That being the case, if there will be nothing done, would not the powers lapse at the end of the two years?

My contention is that nothing should be done that would embar-ras the action of the government in future regarding these powers. That country is developing rapidly, we need all the power we can get in the city of Winnipeg, and the time may come when the power from these very falls would be most essential to the prosperity, not only of Winnipeg, but of other great towns in the west. When that time comes, the government ought to be in a position to handle that power,

which it could not do if it were tied up by1 the legislation that is now proposed. As I have pointed out with regard to the railway scheme, I think every hon. gentleman who has paid any attention to the proceedings of the committee, knows very well that there is no well defined scheme. If it starts south, say at a point on Lake Winnipeg, or at the mouth of the Nelson, the two points are 150 miles apart, and I do not think it is fair to ask this House to grant a railroad charter without some more definite knowledge than we have regarding where it is going to start and where it is going to end. I would, therefore, ask the minister to defer this Bill in order that the government may be in a position to bring down some well defined policy with regard to these water-powers, and espe-ically the powers outside the province. The government at present has no scheme, the legislation they have does not in any way cover the water-powers outside the boundaries of the different provinces. There are three or four water-powers on the Nelson, perhaps as great as the first powder at Sea falls, and there is not one of these powers protected by the regulations issued by the Interior Department. I think that is a-matter that ought to receive the serious attention of the government before anything further is done.
Looking over the Bill I do not see any limitations within which the company shall start operations or complete them.
The general Railway Act will apply.

I understand that the general Railway Act will apply, but if the company fail to commence its operation within the time limited by that Act and they should come back for a renewal of their charter, there would be no difficulty in getting the charter renewed, because the Railway Committee, since I have been in it, has adopted the policy of automatically renewing charters without any question. There has been some spasmodic opposition to the renewal of these charters, but it has practically had no effect at all. I think the time of the members of this House is too much occupied in fighting the aggressions of those private companies. These private companies introduce Bills that purport to be Railway Bills, but in reality they are water-power Bills. Not only this session, but last session, our time was occupied for days and days fighting these private companies who desired to gain control of water-powers that should be left within the jurisdiction of the various provinces. It seems to me an anomaly that matters affecting the province, for instance of British Columbia, should be decided by members from the
provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Quebec.
The Burrard Inlet Bridge and Railway Company.

It seems to me an anomaly that members from Quebec can settle the terms upon which a radial railway company shall enter the city of Toronto. I think there should be some declaration of policy on the part of the government, laying down stereotyped rules and regulations upon which every company can get its charter automatically on well defined conditions. I also think that a regulation might be made that all these matters should be referred to a sub-committee from the province affected by these railway companies. For instance, if a private railway Bill is brought in affecting the province of British Columbia, that might be referred to a sub-committee of members from that province.
What would the hon. gentleman say if it affected the Northwest Territories? Would he refer it to the member for the Yukon? The Bill now under consideration affects the Northwest Territories alone.

In that event I would suggest that the members from the various provinces in the west be a sub-committee. They know the local conditions better than we do.
Progress reported.

National Transcontinental railway, surveys and construction, $27,000,000.

Would the minister state the character of the work done to ascertain the necessary data with respect to classification for the purpose of tendering?
It would be what is known as the preliminary surveys of the country. The estimates were based on the surface indications found by the engineers and some soundings or borings.

I am asking for information because I am in an unhappy state of ignorance in regard to all these matters. I would suppose that where advertisements were sent our for tenders, these tenders to be based on a schedule of prices for each class of work, it would be absolutely essential for the government to know the character of the country and to have some reasonable idea as to how much solid rock, how much loose rock, how much earth excavation would have to be paid for

in the final result. I am not able to understand how the government could arrive at the conclusion that one tender was higher or lower than another unless they had that information in their possession, and I cannot understand how they could come to a reasonable conclusion about the relative merits of the different tenders unless that information in their possession was reasonably accurate and reliable. The information which the minister vouchsafed to the House this afternoon shows that there are discrepancies of a most extraordinary character. Let me give you one example. On contract No. 1, the estimate was that there was no solid rock. Ninety-five per cent of that contract has been done and the final result has not yet been ascertained, but so far as 95 per cent is concerned, it shows no less than 42,219 cubic yards of solid rock. The estimate showed" 129,379 cubic yards of loose rock. The result, in respect of 95 per cent of the contract shows that no less than 938,729 cubic yards have been returned. The estimates showed of common earth excavation 1,841,152 cubic yards. Ninety-five per cent of the work has been done and in that we find only 520,728 cubic yards. If the information in the possession of the government was so absolutely inaccurate as this seems to have been, how was it possible to come to a conclusion about the tenders. I do not wish to draw any conclusion that is not legitimate, but one can easily see how a tender that was really the highest of all might be accepted as the lowest if the information was no more reliable than it was in this case. What is the minister's explanation?

The explanation so far as I can make it is this: I am informed that the usual practice prevailing in Canada was adopted by the engineering staff, the preliminary surveys made and the general contour of the country shown on the profile, with the approximate quantities of each kind of material in each district.
How were the approximate quantities of loose rock and earth ascertained for these estimates?
I presume they were obtained as on all railways, but not being an engineer I cannot give a professional explanation.
Judging by the results they were never ascertained at all.
I am inclined to think that any one could have shut his eyes, never gone near the country at all, and made as good a guess.

The engineering staff followed the usual practice as I understand Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
it. Mr. Dunn is now in the employ of the Grand Trunk Pacific in a very responsible position, and any engineers that have left us have been picked up by other railways and put in charge of the same kind of work. I believe the engineers were good men. The engineers estimated, and the tenders were based on the approximate' quantities given by the engineers, and the contract was given to the lowest tender on that basis.

If the engineers were good men, and if they followed the practice usual in Canada, I assume it is a practice that must give satisfactory results. I am not prepared to say exactly where the fault lies, but undoubtedly if the original estimates were correct then the charges of over classification must be true. It is utterly impossible to conceive that there is not something radically wrong somewhere. Either the work was done with an incredible degree of incapacity or negligence in the first instance, or else the final classification is not a true classification. Something is inconceivably wrong in the one case or the other. I have had some little experience of this in my profession, and 1 know that no such absurd results as these were ever obtained where the work was properly done in both cases. It seems to be an outrageous condition of affairs. Here is an estimate of 1,841,152 yards of common earth excavation; the contract has now been completed to the extent of 95 per cent and yet we find that the classification of common earth excavation is only 520,726 yards or not quite 30 per cent of the estimate. There is something outrageously wrong in this. Does the minister pretend to tell me that is the way in which other railways are built in this country. I know a little about these contracts and I never heard of anything like this before. I shall be glad to hear what explanation the minister can give.

My hon. friend's point is well taken, but of course,-we cannot tell about the entire classification until the board of arbitrators give their report; and then these quantities may possibly be changed in some respects. In reading over some documents the other day it struck me that the engineers in making their preliminary surveys and estimates might not make their estimate of solid rock, or loose rock open to the same interpretation as that put upon it by the engineers making the excavation.
The great distinction is between earth and rock.
On the surface there might be no solid rock as would be indicated in the first survey.
The rock has to be more than a yard in size.

There is an interpretation in one clause that any material that it is best to move by blasting is solid rock. Engineers classify these things differently from what we would understand, and I find that sometimes an engineer will call a thing solid rock when a layman would not so describe it. But granting all that, I admit at once that to my mind the estimated quantities are not as close to what the real returns are, as they ought to be. There is no use arguing it any other way. But a difference between the estimate and the cost often happens in other railways. For instance, I believe that the Sudbury branch of the Canadian Pacific railway cost 100 per cent higher than the estimate. I am. not saying that was in the classification; I am just taking the cost of the line as a whole. Railway companies in making their estimates often go very far astray but the public do not know about it as they do in the case of a public work like this. To my mind the difficulty is not so much in there being a wrong estimate, except _ that that might lead parliament astray in any case as to what the cost would be, if the country is not paying for more than it is getting.
That is not the question.

It is the question I am talking about, and when the arbitrators make their final examination, I have full faith that the country will pay only for what it has got, and the classification will be properly laid down by the board.

The hon. minister must know that there is a proper way to construct a railway. First, there is a preliminary survey, then there is a location .survey. The duty of the engineers in a location survey is to ascertain not only the quantity in the prisms, but the composition. How do they do that? The hon. minister says that they look at the surface. Not at all. They sink test pits on every portion of the road down to grade line, and they ought to know within ten per cent the proper classification. Fifteen per cent, as the minister stated, is an enormous allowance. What do we find on the first section of the road? No Toek returned by the engineers, and as a matter of fact 40,000 yards of solid rock; an estimate of 150,000 yards of loose rock, and there is 700,000 .yards; an estimate of 18,000 yards of clay or earth excavation, and there is 500,000 yards. How can you have proper tenders when such a state of affairs occurs? The estimates were in such a condition that any one who tendered on the quantities returned by the engineers would have no ehance whatever. The minister
says the same thing has occurred in several cases. I defy him to show a case in which such manifest errors in the location surveys have occurred in the construction of any railroad, unless there is found a pit-hole largely in excess of the quantity the engineers estimated. Strange to say, the prism quantities are nearly correct. The only fault is in the classification, the dividing up. If a man who takes out earth is paid for loose rock, and the man who takes out loose rock is paid for rock, it is the fault of the department or of the engineering staff who superintended the location .survey. When there is 40,000 yards of rock excavation where none was estimated, and when the earth excavated is changed into loose rock excavation, the result is that the contractor is paid three or four times the amount he would have been entitled to if the location survey had been correct. There is something wrong. We have no explantion as to when or how it occurred. Everybody knows that in the construction of a railroad the original estimates of the location engineers are kept in a book, and that every week, while the work is going on, a certain portion of it is checked off. The department ought to have a similar book so that they would know at any time when anything went wrong. We have no explanation whether, when they found that these things were going wrong, the attention of the engineer in charge of the work was drawn to the improper classification or not. We should have some explanation, but we have none. It seems that this thing has gone on without any supervision whatever. The hon. minister says that a final estimate is not made, that the classification is still under consideration. I would like to know from the minister, with regard to this section of the road which we are considering, to what extent the contractor has been paid on these estimates, and whether it is not largely in excess of the original quantity as estimated by the engineers, and whether it would not be possible, even with the percentage retained by the government, and the deposit made by the contractor, to secure the government against any charges of that kind? What is the classification on which the contractor has been paid, and what is the amount reserved, over and above the usual ten per cent, for the purpose of preserving 'to the government any right they may have on the final classification?

The hon. minister has spoken as if the great difficulty in these matters were a distinction between loose rock and solid rock. Why, that is a trifle compared with what the real facts are. The great trouble here is the enormous difference between ordinary earth excavation and either solid rock or loose rock. If you

reduced this down to a mere question of difference between loose rock and solid rock, there would be a very important difference; but it would be nothing compared to the enormous loss to the country arising from the fact that what was represented as earth work is being paid for as either loose rock or solid rock. The minister says that he has no doubt that the thing was done as it is usually done by railway companies. I hope that it was so, and if it was, the hon. gentleman can show us, yard for yard, from one end of that road to the other, what the engineers did before these contracts were made. It is not a question of guess work. The minister has the papers in his possession; why are they not produced? Why have we not these explanations now when we are asked to vote $27,000,000 for continuing this work? Why does the minister not tell us where, and how these discrepancies occurred? It does not require an engineer to know that if these discrepancies worked against the contractors, and the government attempted to enforce the contracts the courts of the land would relieve the contractors from their obligations because of fraudulent representations made on behalf of the government. That is the case, and the hon. minister knows it.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that if the locating engineers estimated that a certain cut contained 75 per cent of rock, and the contractor took the contract under that specification and it turned out only 25 per cent rock, he would have an action against the commissioners for breach of faith?

I say that if you should bring before a court such manifest injustice-in this case it happens to be an injustice to the country-to the contractor, as the result of misrepresentations made, the court would relieve the contractor.

One other question. Is the hon. gentleman aware that in asking for tenders for this work the contractors were not given any information whatever as to what proportion was solid or loose rock or common earth excavation, in any of these different works.
, Mr. J. HAGGART. Is the hon. gentleman certain in his statement?
Yes.

I have had something to do with letting railway contracts. Before a company lets such a contract as this government did, its engineers go over again and again every mile of the work, and by pits and borings and preliminary surveys, they ascertain, as nearly as possible, what is the nature of the ground?
Does the hon. gentleman know that that information was given the contractors when tendering for the work?

If a railway company were undertaking to build a new line through a country such as this-and I have in my mind at this moment a similar work-that company would survey every mile with the utmost care, and they would have, as the government has now, if the minister's statement is correct, they would have a record of the borings and surveys of every mile of that road.
Every 100 yards.

Every mile would be done by sections of 100 yards. They would be able to show the prism measurements, the tests, the pits and borings; and it would be such evident, downright fraud, if the differences were so enormous as they are here represented to be that no court would hold the contractor bound by his contract, because of the evident, wilful, deliberate, intentional misrepresentation and fraud. The hon. gentleman says there are differences about loose and solid rock. Why the great difference is that enormous quantities of earthwork are turned into loose or solid rock-not loose- rock turned into solid, or solid into loose. That is where the cost estimated by this government has been so enormously exceeded. No one pretends for a moment that discrepancies or errors of 15 or even 20 per cent difference would he an indication of anything but carelessness on the part of the staff for which we could not hold the government or a company responsible, but to say that the directors of a railway company would not be responsible for such enormous differences as are here shown is absurd. Why, they would dismiss the whole staff if they were an honest board. They would kick every man out as incompetent unless they were afraid to do it because they were a party to the fraud. There is no business man which does not know that to be the case. I have known that in similar cases of difficult railway construction, the company has sent their staff three. times over the ground. They sent them first and got their estimate, and then sent them over again, and even a third time before submitting their surveys for tenders. Then the contractors would come in and the company got all the benefit of the money they had had expended on these preliminary surveys. But what have we here? The hon. gentleman is not able to produce those preliminary surveys. He does not know that any are in existence. He can only say vaguely that the government have done what companies usually do. He ought to know whether he has

the results of those surveys. If he has, it was his duty to look into them and see who were responsible for this enormous expenditure, wholly unexpected and wholly unauthorized. That is what I complain of. It is no use for the hon. gentleman to ask for $20,000,000 and tell us he has no doubt that what is usually done was done in this case. He ought to know what was done. He ought to have the papers in his office and see whether there are still in the pay of this government men who deliberately falsified the figures or were so negligent that they were even worse than rogues and falsifiers.

I would not dare to follow my hon. friend in his sweeping strictures and denunciations of people as rogues and falsifiers. I am always sufficiently charitable to. consider every man as honest as myself until I find out that he is not. It does not help our argument on either side to call names. My hon. friend is a good railway man perhaps, but I will venture the assertion that there is not an hon. member in this House who has heard him who would think that he has made this clear, and that is that the contractors do not base their estimates on information as to quantities or classification given them by the government..

Is the government estimate submitted them before they tender?
Mr. GRAHAM No. They know nothing about the quantities which the government engineers have figured out.
The government makes certain tests and borings, and estimate as best they can what the classifications eventually will be-is that information not submitted in any form to the contractors?
Partially it is and partially it is not. There is a profile given the contractors and that profile shows the probable findings in different parts of the country.
As the result of your survey?

Yes. But the engineers of any company are supposed to find out for themselves, they are not given the faintest inkling of what quantity' there is of solid rock, no quantities are given at all, there is merely given a profile of what is in the different districts. These are not guaranteed. If the contractors are good business men, they send their own engineers over the territory, and base their tenders on their own information, and not on ours at all, and that is what they nearly always do. The government, or any
company, merely gives them the general character of the country on a profile.
Is this contract let at so much per yard for solid rock, so much for loose rock, and so on?
Yes.

How does the minister account for this extraordinary statement contained in the speech from the Throne:
The eastern division is now ready for traffic_ from Winnipeg to Lake Superior Junction.

It was ready for traffic as I have outlined, and traffic could have been carried over that line for the entire season by the' contractors had the Grand Trunk Pacific desired to make such an arrangement with them. It could be carried by the Canadian Northern bridge over the Red river, connecting with that Dundee branch and running through. The Grand Trunk Pacific, as I understand it, did not care to make that arrangement with the contractors, but traffic could have been carried as contractors do carry on transportation along many lines before they hand their work over as complete.

The statement of the minister is very different from the statement in the speech from the Throne. The speech from the Throne does not say there is still $1,000,000 to be expended upon it, and that by using the Canadian Northern bridge some trains could be run over jt- had the Grand Trunk accepted the offer of the contractors. The speech from the Throne is much more direct:
The eastern division is now open for traffic from Winnipeg to Lake Superior Junction.
Why is it that so absolutely a misleading statement-not to use any harsher term- was placed in the mouth of His Excellency by the government?

I think my hon. friend from Marquette would say that the prairie section was open for traffic, although it is being run under the construction company yet. But, it is open for traffic and running through to Wolf creek.

But this does not even fulfil that condition. I am not concerned with what my hon. friend from Marquette would say, but I am concerned with what His Excellency the Governor General has said, and in this connection the government made him say something that is absolutely untrue. I am inclined to think that His Excellency would be perfectly justified in dismissing all his ministers.
He would make a mistake.

I do not think he would make anv mistake. This section never was open for traffic, and could not have been open for traffic until the government took it over and leased it to the Grand Trunk Pacific. It never has been operated by the contractors; they offered to operate it, but the offer has not been accepted.
It W'as open for traffic, and the traffic did not come.

If the Minister of Railways considers that a fair interpreta-

tion of the language of His Excellency, 1 will not argue any more with him. He knows perfectly well that the people of the country who read* the speech from the Throne understood that the line was- open for traffic in the ordinary course, and in that sense such a statement was absolutely and wholly mendacious and. the Governor General has been led into a very unfortunate position. No fault is to be attributed to His Excellency, because I suppose he is obliged to place confidence in the representations of his ministers in matters of this kind. But why the trouble was taken to put these words into the mouth of His Excellency, when it must have been perfectly apparent that the truth would be discovered within a very short time, is more than I can understand.

It is well to have that statement, but that is not exactly what I wanted to know. I want to get from the minister a statement of the estimated expenditure outside of the contracts, necessary to complete the whole work; for instance, the cost of the Quebec bridge, and the terminals, and everything not embraced in the contracts.

I gave the estimated cost of the Quebec bridge several week3 ago. Outside of the information I have given here. I am not clear as to what my hon. friend wants. The contracts include everything along the line except the steel rails and fastenings, and the steel bridges, and I have given all these.
As far as they have been constructed; but the government has an estimate of what the various items not embraced in the contracts will come to.

What is wanted, in short, seems to be this. We have a statement of what the contractors have already received, and an estimate of what they will receive. Outside of that, some other things are necessary to complete the road, and to put it in running order before it can be handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. What is their estimated cost, outside of the contracts?

It may be a little difficult to get that information very promptly. For instance, take the Quebec terminals- my hon. friend knows that it is not decided yet where they are to be, and it is impossible to say what they will cost.
Give us as much as you can* and tell us what you are leaving out.

Of course, it would be idle to ask for an estimate of what is not definitely decided on; but, apart from that, the minister might give us_ an estimate, mentioning what is not included, but what must necessarily be provided. I would like the minister also to let us know when we meet again whether there is any change in his estimate of the cost of the Western Division.

The Prairie Section is practically finished at the figures already given, and there is no change in the estimate of the cost of the Mountain Section given to me by Mr. Schreiber.
